transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, nice to meet you too. Well, I guess... I mean, the main thing that brings me in is that I just feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. I’m a special education teacher, and you know, it’s a job that keeps you on your toes, but this is different. It’s like... I finish one thing at school, say, wrapping up a lesson with my kids or filling out an IEP report, and instead of just taking a breath for a second like a normal person, I immediately jump right into the very next task. I just can't stop moving. 

And it’s not just at work, either. I get home, and you'd think a guy my age—I'm 58—would want to sit down in his recliner after a long day, but no, I walk in the door, drop my bag, and instantly start cleaning the garage, or pacing around the kitchen, or fixing something out in the yard. I just jump from one thing to the next without ever being able to shut myself off. It’s like the engine is just revving all day long and I don't have the keys to turn it down. My wife says it makes her tired just watching me, and honestly, it's exhausting to live it. I just... I can't seem to stop and just sit still, if that makes any sense?
Lately, have you been needing less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like I don't need sleep, or that I feel, you know, refreshed after only getting a few hours. Actually, it's quite the opposite in a way. I still need a good seven or eight hours, just like I always have. When I finally do manage to crash—which, let me tell you, is a whole ordeal in itself because my brain just wants to keep going and going, thinking about the lesson plans for the next day, or whether I remembered to send that email to the principal, or if the lawnmower needs a new spark plug—but when I do finally fall asleep, I sleep hard. 

And when the alarm goes off at 5:30 in the morning, I don't pop out of bed feeling like Superman, you know? I'm tired. I feel my age. My joints ache a little, and I groggily shuffle to the coffee maker just like anybody else. It's just that once the coffee hits, or once I get moving, that motor kicks back on and it just doesn't stop. So it's not a lack of needing sleep, or feeling like I have this magical endless well of energy. I get exhausted, physically and mentally. It's more that my body and my brain refuse to acknowledge that exhaustion during the day. They just keep pushing and pushing, even when I know I should be tired, even when I *want* to be tired and just sit on the couch. So, no, I definitely still need my sleep. If I didn't get it, I don't know how I'd survive the school day, especially with my kids. They require a lot of patience and focus, and if I'm running on empty, well, that's just not fair to them, is it? So I make sure I sleep, it's just the shutting down part that's the real trick.
Do unwanted thoughts keep popping into your mind even when you try to ignore them?

No, I wouldn't say I have unwanted thoughts popping in, not like... not like things I'm trying to push away or ignore. It's not that kind of intrusive, bothersome thing where I'm thinking about something terrible or something I don't want to think about. It's more just... well, like I was saying before, it's just the volume and the speed of the thoughts. 

It's like, I'll be sitting there trying to grade a stack of modified math worksheets—and let me tell you, grading for special ed takes a very specific kind of focus because you're not just looking for the right answer, you're looking at the *process* the kid used, trying to figure out where the disconnect happened in their reasoning—but while I'm doing that, my brain is just ping-ponging all over the place. I'm thinking about the math worksheet, yes, but I'm also thinking about whether the tires on my truck need rotating, and then I'm thinking about how I need to call my brother back about his upcoming visit, and then I'm wondering if I remembered to take the chicken out of the freezer for dinner, and then I'm back to the math worksheet, but only for a second before I start thinking about a new behavioral strategy for one of my students who has been acting out during transition times. 

It's just a constant stream of *stuff*. But it's all normal stuff, you know? Everyday things, tasks, plans, ideas. None of it is unwanted or scary or weird. I don't sit there trying to block it out because it's bad, I just get frustrated because there's so much of it all at once and it won't quiet down so I can just do the one thing I'm supposed to be doing. My wife calls it my "popcorn brain" because it's just pop, pop, pop, one thought after another. But no, to answer your question, they aren't unwanted thoughts that I'm fighting against. It's just a very crowded, very noisy waiting room up there, and everyone is talking at the same time.
Did you have this same kind of trouble sitting still and keeping your mind on one thing when you were a child?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, this isn't some new development, not by a long shot. It's funny you ask that, actually, because I was just talking to my sister about this the other day—we were going through some old boxes of our parents' things since my mom passed a few years back, and we found all these old report cards from when I was in elementary school. And let me tell you, reading those teacher comments was like looking in a mirror, even fifty years later. 

My mother, she used to joke about it all the time. She’d say, "Tommy"—that's what they called me back then—"Tommy, you practically taught the class from your seat." And she wasn't exaggerating! I was always, always out of my chair. If the teacher was at the chalkboard, I'd be up wandering over to the pencil sharpener, or going to look out the window, or walking over to see what my buddy was drawing on his desk. I just could not stay glued to the seat. And the talking! Oh, the talking. I was the kid who was always blurting things out, cutting in before the teacher even finished giving the directions for the assignment. I just had this... this urgency, you know? Like whatever was in my head had to come out right that exact second, or I'd burst. 

I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—wonderful woman, very patient, which was a blessing for me—she actually put a little strip of masking tape on the floor around my desk. It was my "boundary." But even then, I'd be leaning over the tape, stretching as far as I could go without technically stepping out of it, just to see what was happening on the other side of the room. So, yes, this whole... this engine constantly running, this inability to just sit and be still, it's been part of who I am for as long as I can remember. Long before I became a teacher myself, long before I got married or had any of the responsibilities I have now... long before any recent family changes or stress. It's just... it's just me. It’s always been me, from the very beginning. It's just getting so exhausting to keep up with it now at my age.
Do you tend to worry excessively about everyday things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

Well, no, I wouldn't use the word worry. Not at all. I mean, sure, I think about things constantly, like I was just saying, but I'm not sitting around wringing my hands or feeling anxious about it. It's actually funny you use that word, because people sometimes look at me—my wife, for instance, or even some of the younger teachers in the special ed department, the ones who are fresh out of college and still trying to figure out how to manage a classroom—they'll see me pacing around the teacher's lounge, muttering to myself about the schedule for the upcoming IEP meetings, or checking my pockets three times to make sure I have my keys, and they probably think, 'Oh, Tom's really stressed out, he's really worried about something.' But I'm really not! 

Worry, at least to me, implies some kind of fear, right? Like you're afraid something bad is going to happen if you don't fix it. I don't have that at all. If I'm thinking about... oh, I don't know, the gutters needing cleaning, I'm not sitting there worried that the house is going to flood and wash away in the next rainstorm. I'm just thinking, 'Okay, the gutters need cleaning, which means I gotta get the tall ladder, but the tall ladder is behind the lawnmower in the shed, and the shed needs a new padlock because the old one is rusting, so I should probably go to the hardware store, and hey, while I'm there, they might still have that sale on mulch...' 

You see what I mean? It's... it's a to-do list. It's a very loud, very fast to-do list that's running on a loop at a hundred miles an hour, but it's not driven by anxiety or dread. It's just logistics. It's just my brain trying to organize a million little puzzle pieces all at the
